title: What is a `CHECK` constraint (`CHECK (salary > 0)`, `CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','INACTIVE'))`), when does the DB reject the row (on INSERT or UPDATE that violates), and why is a DB-level CHECK safer than app-only validation (multiple apps, direct SQL, race conditions)?
shortTitle: The CHECK Constraint — DB-Level Domain Rules

s1_definition.profdef: A `CHECK` constraint is a table- or column-level rule that defines a boolean condition the data in a row must satisfy, such as `CHECK (balance >= 0)` or `CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','INACTIVE'))`. The database evaluates the condition on every INSERT and every UPDATE that touches the row and rejects the operation if the condition is false (a null typically passes, since the condition evaluates to unknown, not false). A database-level CHECK is safer than application-only validation because it holds for every writer — multiple applications, batch jobs, and direct SQL — and it cannot be bypassed or lost to a race condition.
s1_definition.analogy: A CHECK constraint is like a hard rule stamped on National Bank of India's ledger itself: "a balance can never go below zero" or "an account's status must be one of ACTIVE or INACTIVE." No matter who walks up to write — the mobile app, the branch system, a nightly batch, or an engineer typing SQL directly — the ledger refuses to record anything that breaks the rule. If one app forgets to check, the ledger still says no.
s1_definition.oneliner: A CHECK is a boolean rule the database enforces on every INSERT and UPDATE, rejecting bad values for every writer — so it cannot be bypassed like app-only validation.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A `CHECK` constraint is a table- or column-level rule that defines a boolean condition the data in a row must satisfy, such as `CHECK (balance >= 0)` or `CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','INACTIVE'))`. The database evaluates the condition on every INSERT and every UPDATE that touches the row and rejects the operation if the condition is false (a null typically passes, since the condition evaluates to unknown, not false). A database-level CHECK is safer than application-only validation because it holds for every writer — multiple applications, batch jobs, and direct SQL — and it cannot be bypassed or lost to a race condition.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A CHECK constraint is like a hard rule stamped on National Bank of India's ledger itself: "a balance can never go below zero" or "an account's status must be one of ACTIVE or INACTIVE." No matter who walks up to write — the mobile app, the branch system, a nightly batch, or an engineer typing SQL directly — the ledger refuses to record anything that breaks the rule. If one app forgets to check, the ledger still says no.

**One line to remember:** A CHECK is a boolean rule the database enforces on every INSERT and UPDATE, rejecting bad values for every writer — so it cannot be bypassed like app-only validation.

sections.s2_technical:
A CHECK constraint carries a boolean expression over the columns of the row. Column-level checks reference one column, like CHECK (amount > 0); table-level checks can reference several columns of the same row, like CHECK (close_date >= open_date). You can also restrict a column to a set of allowed values with CHECK (status IN (...)), which is a lightweight enumeration enforced by the database.

The engine evaluates the check whenever a row is inserted or updated in a way that affects the constrained columns. If the expression evaluates to false, the whole statement is rejected and, inside a transaction, you roll back. A subtle but important rule is three-valued logic: if the expression evaluates to unknown because a value is null, the check is treated as satisfied, not violated. So CHECK (salary > 0) permits a null salary; if you also want to forbid null you add a separate NOT NULL constraint.

Why is a database CHECK safer than validating only in the application? First, multiplicity: in a real system many applications and services write to the same table, and each would have to re-implement and perfectly agree on the same rule; a single CHECK enforces it once for all of them. Second, bypass paths: data arrives not only through the main app but through admin tools, migration scripts, bulk loaders, and engineers running ad-hoc SQL, none of which run your application validation; the CHECK catches them all. Third, race conditions: application checks that read-then-write can be defeated by concurrency, whereas the constraint is evaluated atomically as part of the write itself. The database is simply the one place every write must pass through.

The senior nuances: keep CHECK expressions deterministic and based on the row's own columns — standard CHECK cannot reference other tables or subqueries (for cross-row rules you use triggers or exclusion constraints). Adding a CHECK to an existing large table validates every existing row by default, which can lock the table; databases let you add it NOT VALID first and VALIDATE it later to avoid a long lock. And application validation still has value for fast, friendly user feedback — the point is that it complements, never replaces, the database constraint.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India must guarantee a balance never goes negative and an account status is always a valid value, no matter which system writes.

Problem 1 — a value rule. CHECK (balance >= 0) rejects any insert or update that would drive a balance below zero, so an over-withdrawal cannot corrupt the ledger even if an app forgot to check.

Problem 2 — an enumeration rule. CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','INACTIVE','FROZEN')) rejects any unknown status like 'BLAH'.

Problem 3 — null behaviour and bypass. We show a null passing the balance check (three-valued logic) and a direct-SQL-style write still being caught by the constraint.

The code models a CheckedStore that evaluates these checks on insert and update, an AccountService that performs a withdrawal, and a demo attempting valid writes, an over-withdrawal, a bad status, and a direct write.

check-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/main/java/com/bank/check/
│   ├── CheckDemo.java

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway)
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id      VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    balance DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00
            CONSTRAINT chk_balance_nonneg CHECK (balance >= 0),           -- value rule
    status  VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'
            CONSTRAINT chk_status CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','INACTIVE','FROZEN'))  -- enum rule
);
INSERT INTO accounts (id, balance) VALUES ('SAV2001', 1000000.00), ('CUR3001', 250000.00);

-- Add a CHECK to a large existing table WITHOUT a long lock:
-- ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT chk_balance_nonneg CHECK (balance >= 0) NOT VALID;
-- ALTER TABLE accounts VALIDATE CONSTRAINT chk_balance_nonneg;   -- validates existing rows later
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate   # DB constraints are the source of truth
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: an account with a million rupees, then a mix of valid and invalid operations.

Step 1 — A withdrawal of Rs.50,000 computes a new balance of Rs.950,000. The update triggers CHECK (balance >= 0), which is satisfied, so the row is stored.

Step 2 — An over-withdrawal of about ten crore computes a strongly negative balance. The same CHECK now evaluates to false on the UPDATE, so the database rejects the operation and the balance stays Rs.950,000. Notice the service itself did no pre-check — the database was the guard.

Step 3 — An attempt to set status to 'BLAH' triggers CHECK (status IN the allowed set), which is false, so it is rejected. A change to 'FROZEN' is in the set, so it passes.

Step 4 — A direct-SQL-style insert with a null balance passes, because the CHECK on a null evaluates to unknown and unknown is treated as satisfied. A direct insert with a negative balance is still caught by the CHECK, proving the constraint protects even writers that bypass the application.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 17:44:00 [INFO] inserted SAV2001 balance=1000000 status=ACTIVE
2026-10-25 17:44:00 [INFO] updated SAV2001 balance=950000
2026-10-25 17:44:00 [INFO] withdraw 50000 from SAV2001 → 950000
2026-10-25 17:44:00 [SEVERE] over-withdrawal (CHECK balance>=0 fires) → REJECTED: CHECK chk_balance_nonneg violated: balance < 0
2026-10-25 17:44:00 [SEVERE] bad status value (CHECK status fires) → REJECTED: CHECK chk_status violated: status=BLAH
2026-10-25 17:44:00 [INFO] updated SAV2001 status=FROZEN
2026-10-25 17:44:00 [INFO] inserted TMP0001 balance=null status=ACTIVE
2026-10-25 17:44:00 [SEVERE] direct SQL-style write negative balance (CHECK still catches it) → REJECTED: CHECK chk_balance_nonneg violated: balance < 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  INSERT / UPDATE touching accounts
    │
    ▼
  CHECK evaluation (on the row's own values)
    ├─ chk_balance_nonneg: balance >= 0 ?
    │     true  → allow     false → REJECT     null → allow (unknown ≠ false)
    └─ chk_status: status IN ('ACTIVE','INACTIVE','FROZEN') ?
          true → allow      false → REJECT
    │ all pass
    ▼
  Row written — invalid values impossible for ANY writer (app/batch/direct SQL)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — CHECK Enforcement ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Invariant guard at the data boundary                      │
  │  Specification: boolean predicate per row                  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─ SOLID ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: CheckedStore enforces checks; Service does business.   │
  │  O: new rule = new check method, service unchanged.        │
  │  D: Service depends on CheckedStore, trusts its guard.     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ AccountService           │───────▶│ CheckedStore          │
  │ + withdraw(id, amount)   │ uses   │ - VALID_STATUS: Set   │
  │   (no pre-check!)        │        │ + insert(...)         │
  └──────────────────────────┘        │ + updateBalance(...)  │ CHECK balance>=0
                                       │ + updateStatus(...)   │ CHECK status IN set
                                       └───────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. withdraw 50000 → updateBalance(950000) → CHECK ok
  2. withdraw huge  → updateBalance(negative) → CHECK REJECT
  3. updateStatus(BLAH) → CHECK REJECT ; updateStatus(FROZEN) → ok
  4. insert(null balance) → allow (3VL) ; insert(-1) → REJECT
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A CHECK constraint is a boolean rule attached to a table or column that the data in each row must satisfy, like CHECK balance is greater than or equal to zero, or CHECK status is in the set ACTIVE, INACTIVE, FROZEN. The database evaluates that condition on every INSERT and every UPDATE that touches the constrained columns, and if the condition comes out false it rejects the whole statement. One important subtlety is three-valued logic: if a value is null the condition evaluates to unknown, and unknown is treated as satisfied rather than violated, so CHECK salary greater than zero still permits a null salary unless I also add a NOT NULL constraint.

The reason a database-level CHECK is safer than validating only in the application comes down to three things. First multiplicity: in a real system many services write to the same table, and each would otherwise have to re-implement the exact same rule and agree perfectly; the CHECK enforces it once for all of them. Second bypass paths: data arrives not only through the main app but through admin tools, migration scripts, bulk loaders, and engineers running ad-hoc SQL, and none of those run my application code, but they all pass through the database. Third race conditions: an application check that reads then writes can be defeated by concurrency, whereas the constraint is evaluated atomically as part of the write.

In our National Bank of India ledger we put CHECK balance is at least zero and CHECK status in the allowed set directly on the accounts table. When a withdrawal path once forgot its own balance check, an over-withdrawal that would have driven the balance negative was still rejected by the database, so the ledger never went bad, and a batch loader feeding a stray status value was caught the same way. I also keep CHECK expressions deterministic and based only on the row's own columns, because standard CHECK cannot reference other tables, and when adding a CHECK to a large existing table I add it NOT VALID first and VALIDATE later to avoid a long lock. Application validation still earns its place for fast, friendly feedback, but it complements rather than replaces the constraint. The line I remember is that a CHECK is a boolean rule the database enforces on every INSERT and UPDATE, rejecting bad values for every writer, which is exactly why it cannot be bypassed the way app-only validation can.
